title: ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

reading.body:
An AI system was used to generate a fake news article impersonating a Reserve Bank governor and a real journalist in a staged interview that never occurred. The fabricated article promoted an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform, deploying the system as a direct tool in an investment fraud. The failure happened at the point where the generated text entered circulation without verification that the interview or participants were real.

AI-generated impersonation scams are reported as increasingly common and sophisticated. Scammers use AI to create fake articles, websites, reviews and advertisements that misrepresent endorsements by real public figures including politicians and media personalities. No technical safeguard is described that would have prevented the model from generating false statements about real people and events presented as fact.

It is not established whether the AI model was designed or trained to refuse such requests, whether guardrails existed but were bypassed, or what technical measures platforms hosting the content could have employed to detect it.

reports.title: The fake Alan Kohler interview that shows a type of scam that’s on the rise
AI deepfake scams 'an emergency in the making' as ASIC reports rise in false investment endorsements
ASIC warns scammers are using AI to spin vast webs of deception

summary:
# Summary

A fake online article falsely portrayed Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock having a heated interview with ABC finance presenter Alan Kohler about Boulder Sparhaven, an unlicensed cryptocurrency trading platform. The interview never occurred. This hoax exemplifies a rising trend of AI-generated investment scams that the Australian Securities and Investments Commission reports is becoming increasingly sophisticated and harder to detect. Last year, ASIC removed 19,400 scams total, including 5,476 phishing scams and 7,051 fake investment platforms, representing increases of 182, 279, and 151 percent respectively.

Scammers commonly impersonate well-known Australians including Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, TV presenter Alan Kohler, businessman Dick Smith, and billionaire Gina Rinehart to build elaborate webs of deception using fake news articles, reviews, websites, and advertisements. ASIC advises potential investors to verify Australian Financial Services license numbers through official registers before investing. Alan Kohler has suggested heavier fines for platforms hosting such content and the AI models enabling it would help combat the problem.
